issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction of the appellant-accused under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) should be altered to a lesser offense under Section 304 Part II of the IPC.

facts: The incident in question was a "sudden fight" that occurred without pre-meditation.
The Court found that the scuffle took place in the "heat of passion" and arose from "grave and sudden provocation."
The appellant did not take undue advantage of the deceased or act in a cruel manner.
law: The Court distinguished between murder under Section 302 IPC and culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 IPC.
An act that would otherwise be murder is reduced to culpable homicide if it falls under one of the exceptions in Section 300 of the IPC.

Exception 4 to Section 300 applies to acts committed without premeditation in a sudden fight, in the heat of passion, provided the offender does not take undue advantage or act in a cruel or unusual manner.

Section 304 Part I applies when there is an intention to cause death or a specific bodily injury likely to cause death. Section 304 Part II applies when there is only the knowledge that the act is likely to cause death, but no such intention.
application: The Court applied the facts to Exception 4 of Section 300 IPC and found that all its requirements were satisfied.
Since the incident was a sudden fight in the heat of passion and the appellant did not act cruelly or take undue advantage, the Court determined he was entitled to the benefit of this exception.
This meant the offense was not murder (Section 302) but culpable homicide (Section 304).
The Court then determined that the appellant did not have the 'intention' to cause death, but only the 'knowledge' that his act could cause death, as the incident arose from sudden provocation.
Because the case involved only knowledge and not intention, the Court concluded that the appropriate conviction was under Section 304 Part II of the IPC.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the appellant's act fell under Exception 4 to Section 300 of the IPC. It found that the appellant lacked the intention to cause death, possessing only the knowledge that his act could be fatal. Therefore, the Court altered the conviction from murder under Section 302 to the lesser offense of culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part II of the IPC.

issue.issue_text: Whether the sentence of the appellant should be modified as a consequence of the alteration of the conviction.

facts: The appellant was initially convicted by the trial court under Section 302 IPC (murder) and sentenced to life imprisonment.
The High Court upheld this conviction and sentence.
The Supreme Court re-examined the facts of the case.
law: The Court considered Exception 4 to Section 300 of the IPC, which reduces a charge of murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder if the act is committed in the heat of passion during a sudden fight, without the offender taking undue advantage or acting cruelly.
application: The Supreme Court found that the requirements of Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC were satisfied, as the scuffle took place in the "heat of passion" and the appellant did not act cruelly or take undue advantage.

Based on this finding, the Court concluded that the appropriate conviction was not under Section 302 IPC (murder), but under the lesser offense of Section 304 Part II IPC (culpable homicide not amounting to murder).
reasoning.conclusion: As a direct consequence of altering the conviction from the more severe offense of murder (Section 302) to the lesser offense of culpable homicide (Section 304 Part II), the Supreme Court modified the sentence from life imprisonment to 10 years of imprisonment, stating that this new sentence would meet the ends of justice.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the conviction of the appellant-accused under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) should be altered to a lesser offense under Section 304 Part II of the IPC.
appellant_arguments: The attack was not premeditated or preplanned.
The incident arose from a sudden scuffle that started in the Court of the Executive Magistrate when the appellant objected to the presence of a member of the opposite side.
There was pre-existing bitter hostility and ongoing criminal litigation between the two factions, which provides the context for a sudden fight rather than a planned murder.

appellant_arguments: The sentence of life imprisonment, mandated for a Section 302 conviction, should be reduced to a lesser term appropriate for an offense under Section 304 Part II, as a direct consequence of altering the conviction.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: It is immaterial in cases of provocation which party offers the provocation or commits the first assault.
obiter: Since the point for consideration is very limited in the instant case, there is no need to traverse all the factual details rather those having a bearing on the present appeal.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Considering the factual scenario, the legal evidence, and established legal principles, the court concluded that the appellant's act was not cruel and that he did not take undue advantage of the deceased. The scuffle occurred in the heat of passion, satisfying all the requirements under Section 300 Exception 4 of the IPC. Consequently, the appellant is entitled to the benefit of this exception, and the appropriate conviction is under Section 304 Part II IPC instead of Section 302 IPC.
legal_tests_applied: To claim the benefit of Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC, it must be shown that: 1) there was a sudden quarrel and no premeditation; and 2) the offender has not taken undue advantage or acted in a cruel or unusual manner. The expression 'undue advantage' means 'unfair advantage'.
policy_considerations: The legal principle behind Exception 4 (sudden fight) is the recognition that a 'heat of passion' can cloud a person's sober reason and urge them to commit acts they would not otherwise do, which distinguishes it from a premeditated act, even if it doesn't involve a total deprivation of self-control as in Exception 1 (grave and sudden provocation).

The application of doctrines like sudden and grave provocation cannot be based on a rigid, universally applicable construction. The court must examine the specific facts of each case from the perspective of a person of reasonable prudence to determine if the circumstances could lead to a temporary loss of self-control.
